standard.title: Create works that communicate ideas
standard.description: create arts works that communicate ideas
standard.prior_knowledge: No formal prior knowledge assumed. Students bring physical play, movement, and imaginative storytelling from everyday experience.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students create arts works — including dance — that communicate ideas drawn from personal or social experience.

nodes.label: Ideas as starting points
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify an idea from lived experience or imagination to use as a starting point for movement.
nodes.minimum_width: One lived experience or familiar story used as a prompt for movement exploration.
nodes.typical_width: A range of starting points explored — favourite activities, games, animals, or familiar stories — to generate movement ideas.
wider: Use stimuli from multiple modalities — music, objects, tactile materials, or imagery — to generate contrasting movement ideas
Draw on stories and characters from their cultural communities as starting points for movement creation
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a clear idea-to-movement connection, students produce movement without communicative intent — subsequent choreography and sharing nodes lack the anchor they require.

response_modes.reason: Help students articulate what their movement is 'about' — the link between an idea and a physical response. Use prompts: 'What does this look like?', 'Show me how that feels in your body'.
More starting-point types (sensory, narrative, observational) build richer imaginative repertoire for movement generation.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Foundation students who explore multiple stimulus types early develop a transferable habit of connecting ideas to movement — this pays forward across all subsequent arts strands.
success_criteria: Student can name or show the idea their movement is communicating
Student produces at least one distinct movement response to a given prompt

nodes.label: Experimenting with movement
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explore and vary movement possibilities — including body shape, level, direction and dynamics — in response to an idea.
nodes.minimum_width: Exploration of one or two movement qualities (e.g. high/low, fast/slow) applied to a single idea.
nodes.typical_width: Sustained movement exploration across body parts, levels, locomotor and non-locomotor movement, and contrasting dynamics — e.g. heavy/light, fast/slow, big/small.
wider: Explore movement inspired by tactile qualities of materials (rough, smooth, spikey) — translating sensation into movement
Improvise movement sequences that trace shapes observed in the environment (geometric and organic)

response_modes.reason: Students need a physical vocabulary of movement options before they can make intentional choices. Time to play with variation across multiple sessions builds this range.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Students who explore a wide range of movement qualities at Foundation develop a physical repertoire that supports intentional choreographic decision-making in later bands.
success_criteria: Student demonstrates at least two contrasting movement qualities (e.g. high and low, fast and slow)
Student can vary a movement in response to a teacher prompt (e.g. 'make it bigger', 'move more slowly')

nodes.label: Shaping and sequencing
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can organise two or more movement ideas into a simple sequence that communicates an idea to others.
nodes.minimum_width: A simple two-part sequence (start shape → movement → end shape) linked to one idea.
nodes.typical_width: A movement sequence with a beginning, middle and end — using improvised movements selected and arranged to communicate an idea, retell a story, or represent a character or experience.
wider: Repurpose objects or costumes as prompts for imagining and developing short movement scenes
Collaborate with a partner to combine and extend individual movement ideas into a shared sequence
nodes.hinge_reason: The ability to organise movement into a communicable sequence is the foundation of the Presenting strand — students who cannot yet sequence cannot meaningfully share work with audiences.

response_modes.reason: Sequencing is the point at which idea (N1) and movement vocabulary (N2) integrate. Support with visual structure prompts: 'What happens first?', 'What do you do next?', 'How do you end?'

success_criteria: Student produces a movement sequence with at least two distinct parts
Student can describe or show what their sequence communicates (e.g. 'this is me jumping in puddles')
